questions.question: Based on the text, why might the title 'Queen' be considered a bit of a misnomer regarding her power?
questions.answer: The queen does not actually make decisions or 'rule' the hive; her role is strictly biological (laying eggs).
questions.rubric: Full marks if the student identifies that she lacks decision-making power despite the royal title.
questions.source_context: Despite her title, the queen doesn't actually make decisions for the hive. Her main job is simply to lay eggs.

questions.question: What determines the direction of the food source in a forager's waggle dance?
options: The angle of the dance relative to the sun
questions.answer: The angle of the dance relative to the sun
questions.source_context: The angle of her dance shows the direction relative to the sun.

questions.question: Describe the progression of a worker bee's jobs as she ages.
questions.answer: They start as cleaners/feeders, move to guarding the entrance, and finally become foragers.
questions.rubric: Must mention at least two stages: internal hive work (cleaning/larvae) and external work (guarding/foraging).
questions.source_context: Young workers stay inside... cleaning cells... As they get older, they graduate to guarding... The oldest workers become foragers.

questions.question: How many bees contribute their life's work to produce a single spoonful of honey?
questions.source_context: Every spoonful of honey represents the life's work of about twelve bees.

questions.question: What does the treatment of drones in autumn reveal about the hive's priorities?
questions.answer: It reveals that the survival of the colony as a whole is more important than the individual, especially during resource scarcity.
questions.rubric: Looking for themes of 'survival of the colony' or 'efficiency over compassion.'
questions.source_context: In autumn, when food becomes scarce, the workers push the drones out of the hive to conserve resources.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a drone?
options: They collect pollen for the larvae
questions.answer: They collect pollen for the larvae
questions.source_context: Male bees are called drones. They don't collect food, don't guard the hive, and don't have stingers.

questions.question: How far can a forager bee fly from the hive to find food?
questions.source_context: The oldest workers become foragers, flying up to five miles from the hive.

questions.question: What material do young worker bees use to build the honeycomb?
questions.source_context: ...building honeycomb from wax they produce from their own bodies.

questions.question: The author compares the hive to a 'human city.' Based on the text, what is one way they are similar?
questions.answer: Both have highly organized structures where every individual has a specific job or role to play.
questions.rubric: Reference to organization, division of labor, or large populations living together.
questions.source_context: Inside every beehive, there is a world more organized than most human cities... every single one has a job to do.

questions.question: During summer, how many eggs can a queen bee lay in a single day?
questions.source_context: She is the only bee that lays eggs—up to 2,000 per day during summer.
